startup.name: Teaflask
startup.one_liner: Make your product AI native by tomorrow.
startup.description: Teaflask is the AI layer for software companies. It lets any SaaS company put an agent inside its product that carries out tasks for its users, with the controls enterprises require. Customers go live in a day, without a rebuild. Calling a model is the easy part of shipping an in-product agent. The hard part is everything around it: streaming, crash recovery, scaling, guardrails, interfaces that match the product, and knowledge that stays current as the code changes. Teaflask handles all of it with no backend changes, and gives product teams visibility into how their users actually use the product.

yc_acceptance.basis: Start from about 1 percent of applicants with a band of 0.6 to 2 percent (references/yc_acceptance.md). Up: a clear enterprise pain with named technical detail (streaming, crash recovery, guardrails) that reads as founder experience, and fit with the agent infrastructure theme YC funds. Down: a solo founder (102 of 662 researched solo, shutdown 21 percent against 17 percent for two), no stated traction, a crowded embedded copilot category. Net about 3 percent.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly say no because a single founder with no stated customers is selling a horizontal agent layer that looks copyable by model vendors and open source SDKs. The interview would test whether any SaaS company has paid for this, and without a design partner the story reads as a framework looking for demand.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --years 2022-2025 --industry B2B --calibration-only: seed 49% / 59% / 65%, cond 59% (n=126), months_to_seed 3 / 7 / 15 (n=74). Tag AI cohort: 50% / 61% / 67%. Dev tools tag 2022-2025: seed 50% / 55% / 59%.
anchors.adjustment_reason: The 59% anchor is for ever reaching seed. The forecast window is 11.4 months (from 2026-04-06 to 2026-11-17), and the cohort median time to seed is 7 months with a 75th percentile of 15 months, so about 60 to 70 percent of eventual seeds land inside it. That gives a window anchor near 0.37 to 0.42, and a round must also exceed $1M, which removes YC-deal-only cases. Set at 0.38, about the window anchor, with no lift for the hot agent sector. A solo founder, a crowded category and an unproven product offset the demand for in-product AI, so the odds do not rank this company against others.

bands.rationale: Small post YC round of $1M to $3M, usually a pre-seed or angel led round that closes quickly. Cohort data for 2022 and later shows a 25th percentile near $2M, and a team this early often takes the first credible check.
Institutional seed of $3M to $6M, the middle of the 2022 and later table (median $3.2M to $3.5M, 75th percentile about $5M) lifted slightly because only rounds above $1M count here.
Hot sector seed of $6M to $12M. The 2026 winners test found 42 percent of confirmed raises here, but that sample leans to press covered rounds, so this band is held below that share.
Upside band above $12M, reached only with fast revenue or a standout founder story. Rare for a team of this size.

ladder.why_it_fails: Window: 11.4 months, to 2026-11-17. A single founder with a horizontal developer infrastructure pitch has to land design partners and show live customers inside under a year. Investors will ask why a SaaS company would not use an agent SDK such as CopilotKit or the model vendors' own tools. Analogs such as Vizzly and Explo sold embeddable features to SaaS teams and raised only small rounds or sold early. If the first customers are pilots rather than paid contracts, seed investors pass or offer only a sub $3M round.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --years 2022-2025 --industry B2B --calibration-only: series_a cond 26% (n=74), months_to_series_a 22 / 29 / 38 (n=19). Tag AI: cond 23% (n=66).
anchors.adjustment_reason: Same 11.4 month window as the seed step. The 26% anchor is for ever reaching Series A after a seed, but the cohort 25th percentile for reaching Series A is 22 months from batch start, so only about 10 to 15 percent of eventual Series A rounds close inside a window this short. Set at 0.04 for a solo founder team.

bands.rationale: Thin or bridge Series A near the 2022 and later 25th percentile of $11M, taken when growth is real but the story is narrow.
Typical Series A, anchored on the 2022 and later median of $14M to $15M and public medians of $17M.
Upside Series A of $20M or more for a category leader with fast ARR growth, as seen in the top AI cases.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series A inside this window would need paid enterprise adoption across many SaaS customers within months of a seed. Embedded infrastructure companies such as Paragon took more than two years from batch to a $13M Series A, and Explo needed two. A solo team also has to hire before it can scale sales, so a round inside the window is very unlikely.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --years 2022-2025 --industry B2B --calibration-only: series_b cond 16% (n=19); calibration sample all years: 44% (n=126).
anchors.adjustment_reason: This step is for ever reaching a Series B given a Series A, with no time window, because recent cohorts are right censored. Set between the recent cohort figure of 16% (n=19, few years of follow up) and the all years figure of 44%, at 0.14 for a conservative read.

bands.rationale: Modest Series B near the 25th percentile of the 2022 and later table ($25M to $27M), likely a flat or small step up.
Typical Series B, median $37M to $40M with post money around $600M in the sparse data.
Upside Series B for a breakout. Few cohort examples, so the band is deliberately small.

ladder.why_it_fails: Reaching Series B needs a platform with real revenue retention across dozens of SaaS customers. The risk is that model vendors and frameworks absorb the in-product agent layer and that each customer builds the last mile themselves, which caps contract size. Paragon is the best analog and stopped at Series A.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only: series_c cond 36% (n=55) across all years. The 2022 to 2025 B2B cohort has no Series C yet (n=3).
anchors.adjustment_reason: Anchor taken from the all years calibration sample because recent cohorts have not had time. Set at 0.25, about 0.7 times the anchor, since most Series B companies in this category face a very crowded late stage market.

bands.rationale: Series C near the 2022 and later 25th percentile ($35M to $50M), in a flat market.
Typical Series C or D, median $74M with post money about $1.2B.
Late stage breakout round. Very few researched cases, so this is a thin tail.

ladder.why_it_fails: Late stage rounds require a clear platform scale position with revenue across hundreds of software customers. In-product agent infrastructure has no independent winner yet, the surviving embedded infrastructure analogs such as Paragon and Lendflow stopped at Series A, and the more likely path is acquisition by a developer platform or a model vendor before any Series C.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most paths end with the product absorbed by agent SDKs, model vendor tooling or each SaaS customer's own team, so revenue stays at pilots and a solo founder cannot fund the gap. Stalls are common for horizontal infrastructure with long enterprise sales cycles and no wedge customer.

killers.risk: Model vendors, SDKs and frameworks make in-product agents a commodity
killers.evidence: Open source SDKs such as CopilotKit and YourGPT's Copilot SDK already offer in-app copilot building blocks, and cloud vendors ship agent runtimes.
killers.mitigation: Win on the hard operational layer (recovery, guardrails, evals) and sign two design partners with usage data.

killers.risk: Solo founder cannot sell to enterprises and build at the same time
killers.evidence: Team size is one, and the pitch promises enterprise controls and one day onboarding, which needs support and security work.
killers.mitigation: Recruit a technical cofounder or first hire during the batch and focus on five customers.

killers.risk: Customers want to own the agent experience, so spend per customer stays small
killers.evidence: Product teams treat the in-product agent as core product, which favors building in house once models are easy to call.
killers.mitigation: Price on usage and analytics value rather than seats, and show insights customers cannot build quickly.

technical_complexity.rationale: Streaming, crash recovery, guardrails, interface matching and keeping product knowledge current without backend changes is hard to make reliable across many different SaaS products. One person can build a demo in three months but a production grade multi tenant platform is a stretch.

takeover_risk.rationale: Model vendors and open source frameworks already cover pieces and each has distribution to developers. A well resourced rival needs about nine months to ship comparable hosted controls, and SaaS customers can also build in house.

evidence.claim: SaaS vendors are rapidly embedding AI copilots across their platforms, and many frameworks have appeared to serve that demand.
In-app agent assistants that act on a user's behalf are a named product category with several vendors.

roadmap.goal: Show one live SaaS customer with real end user usage.
actions: Integrate with one design partner and measure tasks completed by end users
Write a clear teardown of why building in house is slower
roadmap.proof: A named customer in production with weekly active end users of the agent

roadmap.goal: Three to five paying customers and a repeatable one day install.
actions: Convert design partners to paid contracts
Add a cofounder or first engineer and publish the controls and security story
roadmap.proof: At least $20K monthly recurring revenue and a deployment under one day

roadmap.goal: Show that agent usage grows inside each customer and retains.
actions: Ship product analytics from agent usage that customers cite for roadmap decisions
Hire a sales lead for mid market SaaS
roadmap.proof: Net revenue retention above 120 percent and 15 or more customers

pros.evidence: The description lists streaming, crash recovery, scaling and guardrails, which signals hands on experience building agents in production.

pros.point: Timing with SaaS firms embedding AI
pros.evidence: Vendors are racing to put copilots in products and many lack the team to do it.

brand.name: Teaflask
brand.name_check: python3 -I scripts/name_features.py --score "Teaflask" --era 2022+: invented or proper, 8 characters, 2 syllables, no suffix
strengths: Does not box the company into one product
weaknesses: Tea and flask suggest a beverage brand, not enterprise AI infrastructure
brand.rationale: The name does not hint at the product but invented names like Stripe and Segment worked for infrastructure. It neither helps nor hurts much, and enterprise buyers care about reliability and controls over the name.

narrative.headline: A solo founder selling a crowded agent infrastructure layer, with real demand but a high risk of commoditization.
narrative.general_summary: Teaflask wants to be the layer that puts a task doing agent into any SaaS product in a day. The need is real because every SaaS vendor feels pressure to ship an in-product agent. The trouble is that frameworks, model vendors and in house teams cover much of it, and a solo founder must prove paying customers fast. Over the 11 month window the chance of a round above $1M is near the cohort anchor, and a Series A inside the window is very unlikely. The odds do not rank this company against others.

assumptions: The company is solo with no disclosed traction as of 2026-04-06.
Competition is recorded as of April 2026.

The seed probability is for a window of 11.4 months and a round above about $1M. It does not rank this company against others: in the 2026 winners test the average seed probability was 0.65 for companies that raised and 0.62 for companies confirmed to have raised nothing beyond the YC deal.
Series B and C plus steps are for ever reaching the round, not inside the window. Reaching a round years later is common for companies with paying customers.
Knowledge base coverage: calibration cohorts are 2022 to 2025 B2B (n=150 researched), with funding coverage partial for most, so known-only rates are biased low.
